name: Phase Five: Scale What Works
title: Phase Five: Scale What Works
answer: Phase Five: Scale What Works is the stage where a tool that has passed its pilot is expanded carefully, first to more classrooms or a second school using the same measure, and only then to every classroom. It matters because wider results across different teachers and students are more trustworthy than results from a few enthusiastic volunteers, and because scaling needs tracking, training, support, and clear communication with families.

sections.body: This idea addresses the gap between a successful small pilot and a responsible district-wide rollout. A tool may work for three eager volunteers, but that does not prove it will work for everyone. The phase therefore calls for a wider pilot with the same measure before full adoption. It also treats scaling as an operational task, not just a purchase, so districts must track costs and benefits, plan training and support, and report results to families. The problem it solves is the common failure where a promising tool spreads without proof, support, or accountability and ends up used by only a few enthusiasts.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a district first runs a wider pilot in more classrooms or a second school, keeping the same measure used in the original pilot, and if results hold across different teachers and students, the tool can then reach every classroom. The text does not give separate grade bands, so the sequence applies across grade levels. During scaling, a simple spreadsheet records the tool's cost, the training time, and the measured benefit, such as hours saved or a change in scores. Dividing cost by benefit gives a number the board can compare across tools, and if that number drifts in the wrong direction, the tool goes back under review. Training and support are also planned at this stage, with pilot teachers used as coaches and their time protected, because teachers who join later did not help shape the tool and may need help to use it well.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no study or formal evidence label for this phase. It makes a practice-based claim that results holding up across different teachers and students are more trustworthy than results from three enthusiastic volunteers, but it does not cite research to support that claim. On the evidence question, this idea rests on practice rather than research as presented in the book.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits on scaling. A tool should not go to every classroom at once, and a wider pilot must come first. Scaling without training and support risks the tool being used only by the same small group of enthusiasts. The return-on-investment number is a trigger for review, not an automatic approval, and when it drifts in the wrong direction the tool goes back under review. Decisions about whether to widen, scale, or return a tool to review stay with the district and the board, and families should receive a short summary of what was tested, what happened, and what the district decided.
